sections.h2: What should a New Jersey seller know about the state before choosing a city or county guide?
sections.html:
New Jersey is small, crowded and divided into many local governments, so the rules that touch a sale change more by town and county than by state. Wikipedia lists it as the fifth-smallest state by land area at 7,354 square miles, with 21 counties and 564 municipalities, and every New Jersey county counts as urban for Census Bureau purposes. Because all land sits inside a municipality, almost every seller deals with a town-level tax office, a town-level construction office and a county-level clerk.

The July 2025 Census estimate counts 9,548,215 residents, compared with 9,288,994 in the 2020 count. That spread of people over a small area is why a seller in a dense Hudson County town and one in a Sussex County borough can face very different buyer pools, even though the same state forms apply to both.

Pick the guide that matches the town and county where the house stands, then use the statewide topics below for the parts that are the same everywhere.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers say about New Jersey housing?
sections.html:
Census QuickFacts offers a statewide look at ownership and cost. Treat it as a benchmark, because town values vary widely.

sections.h2: Which New Jersey counties hold the most people, and how do regions differ?
sections.html:
The six largest counties by the 2020 census, according to Wikipedia's county table, are Bergen with 955,732 residents, Essex with 863,728, Middlesex with 863,162, Hudson with 724,854, Monmouth with 643,615 and Ocean with 637,229. At the other end, Salem County had 64,837.

The state's geography shapes what a seller sees.

  • Northeast and the Gateway Region: closest to Manhattan, with up to a million residents commuting daily, according to Wikipedia.
  • Skylands: the wooded, rural and mountainous northwest, where High Point in Sussex County is the highest elevation at 1,803 feet.
  • Pine Barrens: the pine and oak forest of the southern interior, with a lower population density than most of the state.
  • Jersey Shore: a coastline reached by the Garden State Parkway, with homes exposed to nor'easters and occasional tropical storms, including the 2012 hurricane landfall.

The state is broadly divided into North, Central and South Jersey, though some residents do not treat Central Jersey as a region of its own.

sections.h2: How do property tax appeals and relief programs work across the state?
sections.html:
The appeal calendar is statewide with a few county exceptions. The Division of Taxation says every owner may petition the board of taxation, and petitions must be filed and received by April 1, or May 1 where a municipality did a revaluation or reassessment.

Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth Counties follow an alternative calendar with a January 15 deadline. Owners of property assessed above $1,000,000 can go straight to the Tax Court of New Jersey, and a county board decision can be appealed to Tax Court within 45 days.

The Division also runs Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ, and municipalities handle a $250 deduction for seniors and disabled persons, a $250 veteran deduction, and a disabled veteran exemption. The application deadline for the 2025 cycle was November 2, 2026, and the statewide rules are explained in the state homestead and relief guide.

A county guide covers local assessors and boards of taxation, so check the county page for contact details instead of relying on a statewide number.

sections.h2: What does a New Jersey seller pay at closing?
sections.html:
The Division of Taxation's buying and selling guide says no sales tax is due on a home sale and that sellers pay a 1 percent Realty Transfer Fee, with buyers paying an extra 1 percent on sales of $1 million or more. The Division's realty fee page lists the schedule in dollars per $500 of consideration, with a Graduated Percent Fee on residential sales over $1,000,000.

  • Deed recording: every seller furnishes a GIT/REP form with the deed.
  • Residents: use GIT/REP-3 and report any gain on the NJ-1040.
  • Nonresidents: pay an estimated tax of 2 percent of the price or 8.97 percent of net gain unless an exemption applies.
  • Principal residence: up to $250,000 of gain can be excluded, or $500,000 for joint filers meeting the ownership and use tests.

Exemptions from the transfer fee include deeds between spouses or between parent and child, and deeds from an executor to an heir under a will or intestacy.

sections.h2: How does foreclosure work in New Jersey?
sections.html:
New Jersey is a judicial foreclosure state, so a lender has to go through the court. NJ Courts says the lender first sends a Notice of Intent to Foreclose, and the debtor has 30 days from receipt to pay or arrange something else. The complaint follows, and a defendant who wants to contest has 35 days to answer.

After default and final judgment, the court issues a writ of execution and the county sheriff has 150 days to auction the property. Debtor and lender may each request stays, and after the sale the debtor has 10 days to redeem. Free foreclosure mediation exists, and the court cautions against loan modification and rescue scams.

A homeowner who sells before the sheriff's sale avoids the auction. Court filing fees listed by NJ Courts are $405 for a complaint, $175 for an answer and $50 for a motion.

sections.h2: How do rental and eviction rules affect a sale?
sections.html:
A house with a tenant carries the tenancy with it. The statewide Anti-Eviction Act, N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 and following, requires good cause to remove a residential tenant, and cases are heard in the Special Civil Part of Superior Court.

Only a Special Civil Part officer may carry out an eviction. The court's published filing cost is $50 for one defendant, and the trial date is at least 21 days after service. Foreclosure does not by itself force out a tenant with a valid lease.

The separate notice-length rules, the court steps and the tenant defenses each have their own statewide guide, which a landlord-seller should read before setting a closing date.

sections.h2: Where do local rules change from town to town?
sections.html:
Rent control is the clearest example. The Department of Community Affairs says New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but a municipality may adopt an ordinance, and the local rent control board or municipal clerk can say whether a unit is covered.

Property tax relief that depends on a municipality, such as the senior and veteran deductions, is filed with the local assessor or collector. County-level offices, including the county clerk and the county board of taxation, vary in forms, fees and hours, so the county guides cover those.

Ask the municipal tax collector for the current tax bill and the construction or code office for any open permits before listing. Those two requests catch most surprises that slow a closing.

faqs.q: How many counties and municipalities does New Jersey have?
faqs.a: New Jersey has 21 counties and 564 municipalities, according to Wikipedia. All land in the state belongs to a municipality, so every property has both a town tax office and a county clerk.

faqs.q: What is the median home value in New Jersey?
faqs.a: QuickFacts lists $454,400 as the 2020-2024 median for owner-occupied housing. Local medians differ from town to town, so use that figure only as a statewide benchmark.

faqs.q: When is the property tax appeal deadline in New Jersey?
faqs.a: April 1 for most counties, or May 1 where the town did a revaluation, per the Division of Taxation. Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth Counties use a January 15 deadline.

faqs.q: Who pays the Realty Transfer Fee on a New Jersey home sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays it at closing. The Division of Taxation's guide says sellers pay a 1 percent fee on home sales and buyers pay an extra 1 percent when the price is $1 million or more.

faqs.q: Is foreclosure handled by the court in New Jersey?
faqs.a: Yes. New Jersey is a judicial foreclosure state, so the lender must file in court, and the county sheriff runs the auction after a final judgment and writ of execution.
